planTrip.subtitle: Everything you need to know before traveling to Vietnam

visa.title: Visa & Entry Requirements
visa.summary: E-visa, visa exemptions and entry formalities.

sections.heading: E-Visa
sections.body: Most travelers can apply for a 90-day single or multiple-entry e-visa online. Processing usually takes 3-5 working days. Apply only through the official government portal.

sections.heading: Visa Exemptions
sections.body: Citizens of several countries can enter Vietnam visa-free for a limited period (typically 15-45 days). Check the latest exemption list before you travel.

sections.heading: Entry Formalities
sections.body: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from the date of entry. Prepare a return ticket and proof of accommodation for immigration checks.

weather.title: Weather & Best Time to Visit
weather.summary: Seasonal guide for North, Central and South Vietnam.

sections.heading: North (Hanoi, Sapa, Ha Long)
sections.body: Cool winters (Dec-Feb, 15-20°C), hot summers (May-Aug). Best time to visit: October-December when skies are clear and cool.

sections.heading: Central (Da Nang, Hoi An, Hue)
sections.body: Hot and dry February-May; rainy season September-November with possible typhoons. Best time to visit: February-May.

sections.heading: South (Ho Chi Minh City, Mekong, Phu Quoc)
sections.body: Tropical with two seasons: dry December-April, rainy May-November (usually afternoon showers). Best time to visit: December-April.

getting-around.title: Getting Around
getting-around.summary: Flights, trains, buses and local transport.

sections.heading: Domestic Flights
sections.body: Quick and affordable for long distances (Hanoi-Ho Chi Minh City ~2 hours). Book early for the best fares on Vietnam Airlines, Vietjet and Bamboo Airways.

sections.heading: Trains
sections.body: The Reunification Express runs the length of the country - scenic and comfortable for overnight legs between Hanoi, Hue, Da Nang and Ho Chi Minh City.

sections.heading: Local Transport
sections.body: Ride-hailing apps (Grab, Xanh SM), metered taxis, and city buses cover most urban areas. Renting a motorbike requires an international driving permit.

accommodation.title: Accommodation Guide
accommodation.summary: Hotels, homestays and resorts for every budget.

sections.heading: Hotels & Resorts
sections.body: From international 5-star chains to boutique hotels. Beach resorts are concentrated in Da Nang, Nha Trang, Phu Quoc and Quy Nhon.

sections.heading: Homestays
sections.body: A great way to experience local life, especially in Sapa, Ha Giang and the Mekong Delta. Book family-run homestays for authentic meals and cultural exchange.

sections.heading: Budget Options
sections.body: Hostels and guesthouses are widely available in tourist areas at very competitive prices, often with free breakfast and tour booking services.

health-safety.title: Health & Safety
health-safety.summary: Travel insurance, vaccinations and emergency contacts.

sections.heading: Travel Insurance
sections.body: Comprehensive travel insurance with medical coverage is strongly recommended. Check that your policy covers adventure activities if you plan trekking or diving.

sections.heading: Vaccinations & Health
sections.body: Consult a travel clinic 4-6 weeks before departure. Tap water is not drinkable; bottled water is cheap and everywhere. Use sunscreen and stay hydrated in the heat.

sections.heading: Emergency Contacts
sections.body: Police 113, Fire 114, Ambulance 115. Tourist police are available in major cities. Keep copies of important documents separate from originals.

getting-to-vietnam.title: Getting to Vietnam
getting-to-vietnam.summary: Airports, arrival logistics, border crossings and what to arrange before you arrive.

sections.heading: By air
sections.body: International flights reach Noi Bai (Hanoi), Tan Son Nhat (Ho Chi Minh City), Da Nang and Phu Quoc airports, with connections through major Asian hubs. Long-haul travellers typically transit via Singapore, Bangkok, Hong Kong or other regional gateways.

sections.heading: Before you book
sections.body: Check visa and entry requirements first — most nationalities need a visa or e-visa, and rules change from time to time. See the visa guide for details, then book flights (flexible tickets are wise during holiday periods).

sections.heading: By land
sections.body: Cambodia, China and Laos share land borders with Vietnam. International travellers can cross only at official checkpoints; confirm current entry rules and arrange your visa before travelling to the border.

sections.heading: Once you land
sections.body: Airport buses, taxis and ride-hailing apps serve the major airports. For onward domestic flights, trains or buses, book ahead during holidays and peak season — Tet is the busiest period of the year.

money-costs.title: Money & Costs
money-costs.summary: Currency, payments, ATMs, budgeting and tipping — the practical money basics.

sections.heading: Currency
sections.body: The Vietnamese dong (VND) is the official currency. Prices are often quoted in thousands of dong; polymer banknotes are the norm and coins are rarely used in everyday change.

sections.heading: Payments
sections.body: Cash is the most flexible option, especially at markets, street stalls and smaller shops. Cards are widely accepted at hotels, mid-range and upmarket restaurants, and larger stores. ATMs are common in cities and towns — tell your bank before travelling to avoid card blocks.

sections.heading: Budgeting
sections.body: Costs vary widely by season, city and comfort level, so there is no single daily figure. Accommodation and internal transport fill up and cost more during peak season and holidays — book ahead. Keep some cash for markets, street food and short motorbike taxi rides.

sections.heading: Tipping & prices
sections.body: Tipping is appreciated but not obligatory: rounding up a bill or leaving small change is a common gesture, and guides or drivers are often tipped after a good day. Bargaining is normal in markets — keep it friendly, and agree prices in advance for rides where meters are not used.

etiquette.title: Travel Etiquette & Local Customs
etiquette.summary: A few simple manners that help you get a warmer welcome everywhere you go.

sections.heading: Greetings & respect
sections.body: A smile and a polite greeting go a long way. Vietnamese people are generally warm with visitors; showing respect to elders and keeping a calm, friendly tone is appreciated in daily interactions.

sections.heading: Dress at religious sites
sections.body: When visiting pagodas, temples, churches and mosques, cover your shoulders and knees and avoid loud behaviour. Remove your shoes when asked, at doorways and before shrines.

sections.heading: Photography
sections.body: Ask permission before photographing people, especially in rural communities, markets and during ceremonies. Some sites and villages prohibit photos — follow signs and local guidance.

sections.heading: Everyday manners
sections.body: Remove your shoes when entering someone's home, and accept drinks or gifts with both hands as a polite gesture. Keep disagreements calm and private — public arguments are considered impolite.

accessible-travel.title: Accessibility Information
accessible-travel.summary: Practical notes for travellers with disabilities — honest about what varies and what to arrange in advance.

sections.heading: Plan ahead
sections.body: Accessibility varies widely between modern hotels, city centres and rural areas. Tell us or your accommodation about your needs in advance — reliable information is easier to arrange before arrival than on the spot.

sections.heading: Getting around
sections.body: Pavements in many places are uneven or busy, and older buildings may lack ramps. Taxis and ride-hailing cars are often the easiest way to move between sights; newer hotels and transport hubs are usually better equipped than older ones — ask when you book.

sections.heading: Beaches & nature
sections.body: Many natural attractions involve steps, sand or rough paths. Ask about access and terrain before booking tours, and consider guided visits where staff can assist.

sections.heading: Getting help
sections.body: Share your requirements through the contact page — we will help match suitable accommodation, transport and activities to your situation.

sustainable-travel.title: Sustainable & Responsible Travel
sustainable-travel.summary: Small choices that keep Vietnam's landscapes, heritage and communities thriving for future visitors.

sections.heading: Reduce plastic
sections.body: Carry a reusable water bottle and bag, decline single-use straws and bags where you can, and refill at your hotel instead of buying small bottles every day.

sections.heading: Respect nature & heritage
sections.body: Stay on marked trails, take your rubbish with you, and leave stones, shells and artefacts where they belong. Keep a respectful distance from wildlife and never buy products made from endangered species.

sections.heading: Choose responsibly
sections.body: Pick licensed tour operators and boat crews who follow safety and environmental rules. In craft villages, buy directly from makers so more of the money stays in the community.

sections.heading: Support communities
sections.body: Stay in locally run homestays, eat at family-run places and learn a few words of Vietnamese — small gestures make a real difference. Always ask before photographing people or entering private spaces.

news.title: News & Stories
news.subtitle: Press releases and travel stories from across Vietnam

record-arrivals-2026.title: Vietnam welcomes record international arrivals in the first half of 2026
record-arrivals-2026.excerpt: Visitor numbers climb as new air routes and a simplified e-visa process make Vietnam easier to reach than ever.
content: International arrivals reached a new high in the first six months of 2026, driven by additional direct flights from Northeast Asia and Europe and continued growth in regional connectivity.
The national tourism organisation credited a simplified e-visa process and year-round events programming for the uptick, with heritage destinations such as Ha Long Bay, Hoi An and Hue leading demand.
Authorities said the focus for the rest of the year would be sustainable visitor management at popular sites and support for community-based tourism projects in the highlands.

hanoi-street-food-48h.title: 48 hours in Hanoi: a street-food love letter
hanoi-street-food-48h.excerpt: Two days, one neighbourhood at a time — where to eat pho, bun cha and egg coffee in the capital's Old Quarter.
content: Start early at a sidewalk pho stall where the broth has been simmering since before dawn, then walk it off around Hoan Kiem Lake while the city wakes up.
Lunch means bun cha over charcoal in the Old Quarter, followed by an egg coffee in a hidden courtyard cafe — sweet, strong and perfectly suited to a humid afternoon.
Dinner belongs to the grills of Ta Hien street, where plastic stools spill onto the pavement and cold beer flows. Leave room for a late banh mi from a cart near the train tracks.

hue-festival-programme.title: Hue Festival announces its full programme
hue-festival-programme.excerpt: Performances, parades and light shows will fill the Imperial City during the biennial arts festival.
content: The festival's organisers revealed a programme of more than 60 events spanning music, theatre, visual arts and heritage talks, staged across the Imperial City and the Perfume River.
Highlights include night-time illuminations of the citadel gates, a royal court music revival and an international arts exchange featuring troupes from across Asia and Europe.
Tickets and detailed schedules will be published on the official festival channels, with many courtyard performances free to attend.

fansipan-sunrise-trek.title: Sunrise trek at Fansipan: a beginner's guide
fansipan-sunrise-trek.excerpt: What it actually takes to reach the Roof of Indochina — training, guides and the trail up from Sa Pa.
content: Fansipan at 3,143 metres is achievable for reasonably fit hikers, but the mountain deserves respect: steep sections, changing weather and altitude all add up.
Most treks start from Sa Pa with a local guide, camping overnight at one of the high stations before a pre-dawn push to the summit for sunrise above the cloud line.
Pack layers, rain gear and plenty of water; hire warm gear in Sa Pa if you are travelling light, and allow a rest day afterwards to explore the town's markets and waterfalls.

support.title: Support & FAQs
support.subtitle: Answers to the questions travelers ask most

faqs.q: Do I need a visa to visit Vietnam?
faqs.a: Many nationalities can enter Vietnam visa-free for a limited period, and most others can apply online for an e-visa before departure. Requirements change often, so check the official e-visa portal or your nearest Vietnamese embassy for your nationality before booking flights.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: Vietnam spans three regions with different climates. Generally December to April is the driest period across much of the country: the north is pleasant from October to April, the centre from February to May, and the south from December to April. Check the regional forecast for your travel window.

The Vietnamese đồng (VND) is the local currency. Cash is handy for markets, street food and small shops; cards are widely accepted at hotels, restaurants and stores in major cities. ATMs are common in cities and tourist areas.

Short domestic flights connect distant cities quickly, trains run along the coast, and long-distance buses are budget-friendly. In cities you can use taxis, ride-hailing apps and public buses. For shorter hops, motorbike rentals and walking work well.

Vietnam is generally safe for visitors, with low violent crime. Take normal precautions against pickpocketing in crowded places, be careful crossing busy streets, and keep an eye on your belongings. Travel insurance is recommended.

Local SIM cards and eSIMs with data are affordable and widely available at airports and convenience stores. Wi-Fi is common in hotels, cafes and restaurants. Buy from official carriers and keep your passport handy for SIM registration.
Vietnam runs on 220V, 50Hz power. Sockets commonly accept two flat pins (type A) or two round pins (type C) — bring a universal adapter if your plugs differ.

faqs.q: Will I be able to communicate?
faqs.a: Vietnamese is the official language. English is widely spoken in tourist areas, hotels and larger cities; elsewhere a few basic phrases and a translation app go a long way. Signs at popular destinations often include English.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy & Terms of Use
privacy.subtitle: How we handle your data and the rules for using this site

policy.heading: Who we are
paragraphs: This website is operated by the Vietnam Tourism Organization to provide travel information about Vietnam. In this policy, "we" and "us" refer to the operators of this site.

policy.heading: Information we collect
paragraphs: We do not require user accounts, do not process payments and do not run advertising trackers or analytics. We only store the following on your device:
bullets: Your language preference, saved as a cookie so the site opens in EN or VI.
Your saved trip plan, kept in your browser's local storage.
No names, email addresses or payment details are collected by this site.

policy.heading: How we use your information
paragraphs: Your language preference is used to show the site in the language you chose. Your trip plan is used to restore your saved destinations when you return and to fetch their names and details from our content service when you open the trip planner. Trip plan contents are not used for marketing.

policy.heading: Third-party services
paragraphs: To display content we rely on these providers:
bullets: Sanity — hosts our content and images.
OpenStreetMap — provides the map tiles on the destinations map.
Google Fonts — serves the Inter typeface.

policy.heading: Your rights and contact
paragraphs: You can clear cookies and site data at any time in your browser settings, which removes your saved preferences and trip plan. For questions about this policy, contact us through the Contact page. We may update this policy; the date at the top of this page shows when it last changed.

terms.heading: Acceptance of these terms
paragraphs: By using this website you agree to these terms. If you do not agree, please do not use the site.

terms.heading: Accuracy of information
paragraphs: Travel information — including visa rules, entry requirements, opening hours and transport schedules — changes frequently. We work to keep content accurate, but it is provided for general guidance only. Always verify visa and entry requirements with official government sources before you travel, and confirm details directly with service providers.

terms.heading: External links
paragraphs: The site links to external websites that we do not operate. Those sites are governed by their own terms and privacy practices, and we are not responsible for their content.

terms.heading: Intellectual property and changes
paragraphs: Content on this site (text, design, images) belongs to us or our licensors and may not be used commercially without permission. We may modify or withdraw parts of the site or these terms at any time; changes take effect when posted.

mice.intro: Vietnam hosts corporate events of every scale — from regional conferences to incentive trips and trade exhibitions. We help planners connect with venues, build programs and handle the practical details of bringing teams to Vietnam.

services.heading: Conference & exhibition venues
services.text: Major cities such as Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang offer international-standard convention centres, hotel ballrooms and exhibition halls for events of different sizes.

services.heading: Incentive travel programs
services.text: Heritage tours, resort retreats, cruise overnights and team experiences that reward and motivate groups of all sizes.

services.heading: Business visitor information
services.text: Entry requirements, business visa guidance and practical information for corporate travelers.

services.heading: MICE planning toolkit
services.text: Checklists, planning templates and destination guides are available to planners on request — contact our team.

mice.contactText: Tell us the size, timing and goals of your event — we will point you to the right resources.

accessibility.title: Accessibility Statement
accessibility.subtitle: Our commitment to an inclusive website for every traveler
accessibility.commitment: We aim to align this website with the W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 Level AA. Accessibility is an ongoing effort — we review and improve the site as it grows.
measures: Semantic HTML landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) for screen reader navigation.
Keyboard-accessible controls with visible focus states throughout.
Alternative text on content images and ARIA labels on icon-only buttons.
Responsive layouts and resizable text that work from small phones to large screens.
Foreground and background colors chosen for readable contrast.
limitations: The interactive map uses a third-party map widget; some map interactions may be easier with a mouse than with a keyboard.
Some images from external content feeds may not yet have full alternative text.
Automated testing does not cover every assistive technology — we rely on user feedback to catch real-world issues.
accessibility.feedbackText: Found something hard to use? Tell us through the contact page and we will work on a fix.
